extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants/agents) dealing with novelty and claim interpretation under the Korean Patent Act
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for defining claimed inventions, determining claim scope, and assessing novelty (including numeric and parameter limitations), prior art scope, and disclosure/grace-period exceptions under the Korean Patent Act for patent examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty determination per claim
rubrics_metrics.description: When there are two or more claims in an application, the determination over novelty should be made by each claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each claim is evaluated separately for novelty; identicalness of invention is determined by identicalness of the matters described in the claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim-language-first principle for defining invention
rubrics_metrics.description: When the claim language is clear, defining the claimed invention should be made as recited in the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminology in claims is interpreted according to its general meaning and scope in the technical field unless the description explicitly defines a specific meaning; interpretation should be objective and reasonable considering a person skilled in the art at the filing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid limiting claims by embodiments/drawings
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the description of claims is clearly understood, an examiner should avoid limited interpretation just by referencing the description of the invention or drawings in finding technical features of invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Matters described only in the description or drawings should be considered as not recited in the claims; conversely, matters recited in the claims must be considered when interpreting the invention. Example explanations show that broad claim terms should not be limited to specific embodiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of description-specific definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: If an applicant specifically defines a term in the description to be different from its general meaning, the term is interpreted with that specific meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A specific meaning must be clearly and explicitly defined in the specification; mere description of the concept in description/drawings does not automatically create a specific definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling obscure or unclear claim terms
rubrics_metrics.description: If a term disclosed in the claims is obscure and unclear, an examiner should examine whether the claimed invention can be grasped in view of the description, drawings and common general knowledge as of the time of filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the invention can be grasped, the examiner can notify deficiency in specification and novelty collectively; if the claimed invention cannot be grasped even with the description/drawings/common knowledge, novelty examination is not conducted and a deficiency in description rejection is notified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of functional/characteristic claim expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim specifies a product by its work, function, property, or characteristic, such expression should, in principle, be construed as every product that has such function, characteristic, etc., except when specifically defined otherwise in the description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider common general technical knowledge—sometimes products that technically cannot perform the function (e.g., magnets) are excluded from the scope. Examiner should not exclude the function/characteristic from claim features when interpreting the claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation-by-use (use-limited claims) interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a claim includes an expression specifying a product by its use (limitation of use), the examiner should interpret the claimed invention only as a product specially suitable for the use disclosed in the claim, taking into account description, drawings, and common general technical knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a product includes all technical characteristics of the claim, it is not the claimed product if not appropriate for the relevant use or requires conversion. If a product with limitation of use is not suitable for that use, the limitation may have no impact on defining the claimed invention and thus not affect novelty (example: catalogue disclosure vs claimed agricultural use).

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-by-process claim treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: The manufacturing process recited in product-by-process claims is a means of defining the structure or properties of the final product; novelty and inventive step are determined by comparing the product having certain structure or properties defined by all claim limitations (including process).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the manufacturing process does not affect structure/properties (only yield/efficiency), novelty is determined by the final product regardless of process; identical product obtainable by a different process is not novel. If it's difficult to determine process impact, examiner should issue a novelty rejection and consider applicant arguments or evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jepson-type claim construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Even in Jepson type claims (preamble + body), an invention should be specified as a whole including the preamble because claim type does not change technical scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elements in the preamble are not automatically considered publicly known merely because recited there; novelty/patentability is determined on the whole invention including preamble and body; preamble may be construed to limit field, applied product, or exclude scope if the preamble elements were publicly known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'publicly known invention' (prior art disclosure)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'publicly known invention' means an invention the contents of which have been known to an unspecified person without obligation of secrecy in the Republic of Korea and a foreign country before filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination of disclosure scope is based on matters publicly known, considering common general knowledge at filing; if a skilled person can easily arrive at the matters in the reference, those matters are considered publicly known. 'Common general knowledge' and 'well-known art' are further explained (widely known/used technologies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'publicly practiced invention'
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'publicly practiced invention' means an invention which has been practiced under conditions where the contents of the invention are to be publicly known; actual public knowledge by practice is not required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publicly practiced can be determined from subject matter embodied in machinery/systems; matters directly derivable from the practice in light of ordinary skill can be basis for finding a publicly practiced invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'invention described in a distributed publication'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'An invention described in a distributed publication' means an invention which is or potentially be described in a publication; being potentially described means a skilled person can easily recognize the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such inventions can be considered as disclosed in a distributed publication for novelty purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: General considerations on what counts as publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts kept secret by journals are not publications until contents are released; company catalogues produced to promote products are publications except in special unpublished circumstances; thesis publication time is when distributed to public/university libraries after final examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When filing date equals date of publication, claimed invention does not lose novelty except when filing clearly after publication time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of novelty determination (basic comparison)
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty is conducted by comparing matters defining the claimed invention and matters disclosed in the prior art reference and extracting differences; if no difference, claimed invention is not novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claimed invention is not novel when it is substantially or exactly identical to the prior art. 'Substantially identical' is further defined as differences caused by mere addition/conversion/deletion of well-known art that do not practically affect the technical idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty with numerical limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim includes numerical limitations, novelty is governed by specific rules depending on relation between claimed and prior-art ranges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules: (1) New numerical limitation absent in prior art -> regarded novel unless the value can be chosen by skilled person or is hinted by prior art/common knowledge. (2) If claimed range is included in prior-art range, novelty is not negated if criticality of range is shown; to acknowledge criticality requires technical meaning described, embodiments or supplemental materials, and objective experimental proof. (3) If claimed range includes prior-art range, novelty can be denied at once. (4) If ranges differ, novelty generally acknowledged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty for parameter inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Parameter invention: applicant arbitrarily creates a parameter not standard or commonly used, parameterizes it arithmetically using correlations, and employs it as essential claim element; subject matter must be determined from description/drawings/common knowledge before assessing inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty is determined by interpreting the parameter as part of the claim but novelty cannot be confirmed solely because the parameter is novel. Novelty is generally denied if the parameter just experimentally identifies nature/characteristics of a publicly known product or merely changes expression. If reasonable doubt exists about identity with prior art, examiner may wait for written arguments or experimental certificates; examiner must concretely describe grounds for doubt and may propose ways to overcome it. Criteria do not apply if parameter is standard/common/understandable by skilled person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic vs specific expression rules
rubrics_metrics.description: When claim/prior-art use generic or specific expressions, consider following: (i) If claim is generic and prior art specific -> claim not novel. (ii) If claim specific and prior art generic -> claim has novelty unless specific can be directly derived from generic by common general knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided: metal (generic) vs Cu (specific) negates novelty; specific superconducting silver cable may be negated if using silver was commonly known.

rubrics_metrics.name: No combining multiple prior art references for novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparison for novelty shall not be conducted between a claim and a combination of two or more prior art references; combining references is for inventive step, not novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions: when a prior art reference cites a separate publication, that separate publication is regarded as part of the cited reference and may be relied upon for novelty; dictionaries and references used to interpret a term in cited reference are regarded as cited references and can be cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markush/multiple-embodiment claims novelty handling
rubrics_metrics.description: If one or more inventions are described in a claim (e.g., Markush-type), the ground of rejection can be notified on lack of novelty and inventive step for each invention with one single prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When prior art contains multiple embodiments, do not determine novelty by combining two embodiments; combining embodiments in a single reference concerns inventive step, except when one prior art reference is obviously drawn from more than two embodiments considering common general knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant admissions as prior art assumption
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the applicant acknowledges background art in the specification or written argument to be publicly known prior to filing, novelty can be assessed assuming that background art has been published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If special circumstances show the admission was wrong (e.g., prior-filed application not published, company-internal knowledge), and the applicant asserts/proves such cases, the assumption can be reversed and the ground for rejection remedied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure exceptions / grace period (Article 30) requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Article 30, if a person entitled to a patent files within 12 months (6 months for filings earlier than March 15, 2012) after certain disclosures, the invention may be considered not to fall under prior-art disqualifying provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To take advantage, the filer must submit a written statement of intent to the Commissioner of KIPO when filing and submit documents proving relevant facts within 30 days of filing. There are supplementary-fee-related alternative submission periods (e.g., within amendment period, within 3 months of receipt of certified copy of grant, etc.). Purpose: encourage applicants to disclose while preserving patent rights; KORUS FTA extended grace period to 12 months for filings after March 15, 2012.
